source_text:
[standing | m0003]

Your two neighbourhood obligations are a useful decomposition, but they are
not proofs yet. Work on only the first obligation you stated: starting from a
given `rho`-ball around `x`, propose the first justified construction of a
basic product neighbourhood contained in it. State precisely what finite set
of coordinates you choose and what estimate licenses that choice. Do not move
to the second obligation until the Critic discharges this one.

From now on, submit each proposed step to the Critic for acceptance or a
localized objection.

reply_text:
[proof | m0004]

Given \(B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\), choose \(N\ge1\) such that
\[
\sum_{i>N}2^{-i}=2^{-N}<\varepsilon/2,
\]
which is possible since \(2^{-N}\to0\). Constrain exactly \(F=\{1,\ldots,N\}\): for \(i\in F\), set
\[
U_i=\{t\in[0,1]:|t-x_i|<\varepsilon 2^i/(2N)\},
\]
and for \(i>N\), set \(U_i=[0,1]\). Then \(U=\prod_iU_i\) is a basic product neighbourhood of \(x\). For \(y\in U\), each controlled summand satisfies
\[
2^{-i}|x_i-y_i|<\varepsilon/(2N),
\]
so the finite head is \(<\varepsilon/2\); the cube bound \(|x_i-y_i|\le1\) makes the tail \(<\varepsilon/2\). Hence \(\rho(x,y)<\varepsilon\), so \(U\subseteq B_\rho(x,\varepsilon)\).

@proof-critic
